tanya tagaq.bio:
Inuk artist Tanya Tagaq, from Ikaluktutiak (Cambridge Bay), Nunavut, transformed a tradition normally practiced by two singers into a fiercely individual improvisational language. She began experimenting with throat singing after leaving home for high school in Yellowknife, then developed a solo approach while studying visual art in Nova Scotia. Collaborations with artists including Björk and the Kronos Quartet brought that voice into international experimental-music settings, but Tagaq's work has never treated Inuit sound as a texture to be placed inside somebody else's framework. Her performances use breath, growls, cries, melody and physical improvisation to create music that can feel as close to free jazz, metal and contemporary composition as to conventional song form.

The 2014 album Animism became a national breakthrough when it won the Polaris Music Prize, with the jury recognizing a record that refused to soften either its sound or its politics. Retribution followed in 2016 with an even more explicit focus on colonial violence, environmental destruction and bodily autonomy. Tagaq later extended the same creative world into literature with the genre-blurring book Split Tooth, longlisted for the 2018 Scotiabank Giller Prize and winner of the 2019 Indigenous Voices Award for Published Prose in English. On 2022's Tongues, produced by Saul Williams, passages drawn from Split Tooth were set against industrial and electronic production, making the relationship between her writing and music especially direct.

Tagaq's 2026 album Saputjiji pushed that language into ambient, electronic and filmic sound design while confronting militarism, colonial systems and economic power. Across music, writing, visual art and performance, she has become one of the most internationally visible contemporary Inuk artists in Canada without reducing Inuit identity to heritage presentation. Her 2014 Polaris win, 2015 JUNO for Aboriginal Recording of the Year and 2016 appointment as a Member of the Order of Canada reflect the institutional recognition, but her larger importance lies in how forcefully she has expanded the space available to Indigenous experimental art on major Canadian and international stages.
tanya tagaq.directory_summary: Ikaluktutiak-born Inuk artist Tanya Tagaq turned solo throat singing into an uncompromising experimental language spanning voice, electronics, improvisation, literature and visual art. Her album Animism won the 2014 Polaris Music Prize, while Retribution, Tongues and 2026's Saputjiji pushed further into colonial critique, environmental politics and industrial sound. A Member of the Order of Canada and award-winning author of Split Tooth, Tagaq has helped expand the international space available to contemporary Inuit art without separating experimentation from cultural and political urgency.

the beaches.bio:
Toronto quartet The Beaches grew out of a much longer musical partnership than their 2020s breakthrough suggests. Sisters Jordan and Kylie Miller began playing together as children and formed the earlier band Done With Dolls with drummer Eliza Enman-McDaniel before guitarist and keyboardist Leandra Earl completed the lineup that became The Beaches. Named for the east-Toronto neighbourhood where several members grew up, the group developed through years of touring and major-label rock releases, including the 2017 debut Late Show. Their early momentum brought a 2018 JUNO for Breakthrough Group of the Year and established them as a regular presence on Canadian alternative radio.

The band's career changed dramatically after a management and creative reset that put more control over its identity back in the members' hands. Released independently, 2023's Blame My Ex sharpened their guitar sound with new-wave and pop instincts and produced the viral single "Blame Brett." The song became their first U.S. Billboard-charting track, spent an extended run at No. 1 on Canadian alternative radio and helped move the band from smaller club audiences into much larger North American rooms. At the 2024 JUNO Awards, The Beaches won both Group of the Year and Rock Album of the Year, turning what could have been a one-song viral moment into a broader national breakthrough.

No Hard Feelings followed in 2025 and extended that momentum, with "Last Girls at the Party" spending 11 weeks at No. 1 on Billboard Canada's Modern Rock Airplay chart. The group was named Billboard Canada's Women of the Year in 2025, the first band to receive the publication's flagship honour, and won the 2026 JUNO for Group of the Year. The Beaches matter in contemporary Canadian rock because their biggest success arrived after more than a decade of development: rather than being created by a viral platform, they used one viral song to expose a fully formed band, then converted that attention into sustained radio, touring and international growth.
the beaches.directory_summary: Toronto quartet The Beaches turned more than a decade of playing together into one of Canadian rock's biggest recent international breakthroughs. After early major-label success and a 2018 JUNO for Breakthrough Group, the independently released Blame My Ex and viral hit "Blame Brett" pushed them onto U.S. charts and into larger venues. Follow-up No Hard Feelings, repeated alternative-radio No. 1s and JUNO Group of the Year wins confirmed that the breakthrough was built on a durable band identity rather than a single viral moment.
